title: Techcombank Ho Chi Minh City International Marathon 2026: Vietnam's biggest race, and still open
seo_title: Techcombank HCMC Marathon 2026: Course, Entry and Guide
meta_description: Vietnam's largest marathon runs 6 December 2026 through central Ho Chi Minh City. A labelled, AIMS-measured course, a field near 18,000, and entries open until 6 November.
dek: Nine editions in, Vietnam's flagship road race has the field size, the accreditation and the city-centre course to justify the trip -- provided you can handle a pre-dawn start.
verdict: This is the most serious road marathon in Vietnam and one of the few in mainland Southeast Asia with both full AIMS membership [4] and a World Athletics road race label [3]. The course is genuinely central, running past Notre-Dame Cathedral, Independence Palace and Ben Thanh Market before following the Saigon River [1][6], and the field has grown to a scale -- close to 18,000 runners from 64 countries at the seventh edition [5] -- that gives it real atmosphere. Unlike most of the region's August races, this one is still enterable: registration is open until 6 November 2026 [1], a month before the 6 December race date. The two things to weigh are the pre-dawn start, which is a heat concession rather than a quirk, and the fact that a field this size makes the opening kilometres crowded.

sections.heading: The accreditation is the real differentiator
paragraphs: Plenty of Southeast Asian marathons describe themselves as international. Fewer can point to the paperwork. This one is a full member of AIMS, carrying the M/H/R designation that covers its marathon, half marathon and shorter road distances [4], and it holds a World Athletics road race label [3].

The practical consequence is measurement. An AIMS-certified course is measured to a defined standard, which is what makes a finishing time portable -- usable for a qualifying standard, a club record, or simply a personal best you can trust. On an uncertified course you are running an approximation.

It is also, at nine editions, an established race rather than a new one [1]. The organiser, Sunrise Events, has run this long enough that the logistics of closing central Ho Chi Minh City roads are a solved problem rather than an annual experiment.

sections.heading: A course through the middle of the city
paragraphs: The start is at Le Duan and Nguyen Binh Khiem [1], and the route is a road loop through the centre. Runners pass Notre-Dame Cathedral, Independence Palace and Ben Thanh Market, then run a stretch along the Saigon River [1][6].

This matters more than it sounds. A great many large Asian marathons are routed onto ring roads, industrial corridors and river embankments, because those are the roads a city can most easily close. Getting a course through the actual civic centre of a city of nine million is a meaningful organisational achievement, and it is most of why this race feels different from its regional peers.

AIMS publishes no elevation profile and refers runners to the race website for the route map [4]. Ho Chi Minh City is flat, so the course is not a climbing test -- the difficulty is entirely heat, humidity and, in the shorter distances, congestion.

sections.heading: The pre-dawn start, and why it exists
paragraphs: The marathon starts before dawn [6]. This is the same calculation every equatorial-latitude race makes: Ho Chi Minh City in December is still warm and humid, and a marathon finishing in the middle of the day would be a materially more dangerous event.

The trade-off is that you will run a large part of the race in the dark, and the landmarks the course is built around will be lit rather than seen properly. If the appeal is running through a city you want to look at, the shorter distances start later and deliver more of that.

The second trade-off is preparation. Runners who have never raced a pre-dawn marathon routinely get the fuelling and the sleep wrong. If this is your first, treat the schedule as something to rehearse in training rather than improvise on the day.

sections.heading: Field size: the atmosphere and the crowding
paragraphs: The seventh edition drew a record field of nearly 18,000 runners from 64 countries and territories [5], and the race bills itself as Vietnam's largest [6]. That scale is most of the appeal -- a field that size brings genuine crowd support and the sense of occasion that a 900-runner regional race cannot.

It also brings congestion. A field approaching 18,000 across six distances means the early kilometres are slow whether or not you want them to be, and runners chasing a specific time should plan for a start-corral scramble rather than a clean first mile.

The international spread is worth noting for a different reason: 64 countries is a strong signal that a race's organisation, timing and results handling are of a standard that travelling runners will accept.

sections.heading: Entry: open until 6 November
paragraphs: Registration for the ninth edition is open and closes on 6 November 2026 [1], a month ahead of race day. Six distances are offered: the full marathon, half marathon, 10km, 5km, and 3km and 1.5km options for younger runners [1].

Entry fees are tiered by registration phase, and the official fee page was not publicly retrievable at the time of writing -- it blocks automated access. Check marathonhcmc.com directly for the current tier before budgeting, and be aware that later phases cost more, so there is a real financial reason not to leave it to the deadline [2].

For the same reason, treat third-party listings for this race with some caution. Because the official site cannot be cross-checked automatically, aggregator pages for this event go stale without anything catching it -- a general hazard with race listings, and a specific one here.

sections.heading: Who it suits
paragraphs: It suits a runner who wants a properly measured, properly organised marathon in Asia with a course worth photographing, and who is happy to travel for it. It suits anyone chasing a time that needs to stand up, because the certification means it will.
It suits a heat-averse runner poorly, whatever the start time -- December in Ho Chi Minh City is not cool, and pre-dawn only softens the problem rather than removing it.

And it suits the impatient: unlike much of the region's calendar, you can still enter this one. That is worth something in August, when most of the year's remaining marathons have already closed their books.

faqs.question: Is registration still open for the Techcombank HCMC Marathon 2026?
faqs.answer: Yes. Registration for the ninth edition is open and closes on 6 November 2026, a month before the 6 December race date. Fees are tiered by registration phase, so entering earlier costs less. Register through the official site at marathonhcmc.com rather than a third-party listing.

faqs.question: When and where is the Techcombank HCMC Marathon held?
faqs.answer: The ninth edition takes place on Sunday 6 December 2026 in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. The start line is at Le Duan and Nguyen Binh Khiem in the city centre, and the route is a road loop through central districts before following the Saigon River.

faqs.question: What distances does the race offer?
faqs.answer: Six distances are available: the full marathon at 42.195km, the half marathon at 21.1km, plus 10km and 5km road races and shorter 3km and 1.5km options aimed at younger runners. This spread makes the event accessible to families as well as competitive club runners.

faqs.question: Is the Techcombank HCMC Marathon course certified?
faqs.answer: Yes. The race is a full member of AIMS with M/H/R designation covering its marathon and half marathon, and it carries a World Athletics road race label. That means the course is measured to an international standard, so finishing times are valid for qualifying purposes.

faqs.question: What is the course like and how hard is it?
faqs.answer: The route is flat, running through central Ho Chi Minh City past Notre-Dame Cathedral, Independence Palace and Ben Thanh Market before joining the Saigon River. The difficulty is not elevation but heat and humidity, which is why the marathon starts before dawn.

editorial_notes: Written 2026-08-05 from primary and independent sources, each claim traced to its numbered citation. No pull quotes: no source carries a verbatim on-record quote from a named official. No rating: the 2026 edition had not been run at the time of writing. Entry fee amounts are deliberately not stated -- the official fee page blocks automated access and no independent source carried current figures, so quoting a number would have meant guessing. Registration was verified as open with a 6 November 2026 deadline, and the entity's registration_deadline was set accordingly.
